tier_reason: README 'Benchmark Results' table compares json.cpp to nlohmann::ordered_json. The benchmark code is public (json_test.cpp BENCH(2000, ...) macro and nlohmann/json_test.cpp), and the README states gcc 13.2 -O3 on Ubuntu 24.04 with an AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO 7995WX, so it meets A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README says '2x-3x faster' and that parsing the json_test.cpp example was '3x faster' than nlohmann. Benchmark table (ns, 2000x each), json.cpp vs nlohmann::ordered_json: object_test 71 vs 202, deep_test 226 vs 659, parse_test 675 vs 1928, round_trip_test 1309 vs 4258, json_test_suite 10462 vs 16617, i.e. ~2.8x / 2.9x / 2.9x / 3.25x / 1.6x (derived from page data). README also claims '10x' faster compile (~120 ms vs >=1200 ms) and '10x less code' (json.h 233 + json.cpp 1,303 lines vs nlohmann json.h 24,766 lines).
corrections.caveats: First-party 'quick and dirty' benchmark run by the author on the author's hardware; no independent reproduction found. Compiler/CPU are stated in the README intro bullet, not next to the table. json_test_suite() was changed locally to include only the successful cases; the README says the unmodified test shows a 39x (not 3x) advantage for json.cpp that the authors 'haven't figured out how to explain yet'. Needs Google double-conversion as a dependency.

notes: Speed numbers match the README exactly. I fixed claimed_speedup because the record's '~100x fewer source lines' counted only json.h (233 lines) against nlohmann's json.h; the README itself says 10x, since json.cpp adds 1,303 lines. GitHub reports the license as NOASSERTION, but the LICENSE file is Apache-2.0 text (Mozilla, 2024), so the record's license is correct.

tier_reason: README Benchmarks tables compare scn::scan to std::stringstream and sscanf. The code is in the benchmark/ directory (CMake option SCN_BENCHMARKS), and the README states clang 18.1.1, -O3 -DNDEBUG -march=haswell with LTO, on an AMD Ryzen 7 5700X, so it meets A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Average ns, scn::scan vs std::stringstream vs sscanf: int 27.1 vs 85.5 vs 272.7; double 59.7 vs 283 vs 432; string word 24.5 vs 134 vs 58.4. That is ~3.2x (int), ~4.7x (double) and ~5.5x (string) faster than std::stringstream (derived from page data). The same tables show std::from_chars is faster than scn::scan (int 10.9 ns, double 23.0 ns).
corrections.caveats: Numbers come from the project's own in-repo benchmark suite, run 2024-05-23 at commit 3fd830de; no third-party reproduction. The README does not say whether std::stringstream came from libstdc++ or libc++. scn::scan beats iostream and sscanf but loses to std::from_chars and fast_float::from_chars, and only roughly matches strtol (scn::scan_int).

notes: Every number matches the README. The record's last_commit (2026-09-23) was the repo's pushed_at; the latest commit on the default branch (master) is 2025-10-29, which still counts as active. The category 'serialization-json' does not fit a scanf/iostream replacement, but category is not a correctable field.

tier_reason: The README claims 5x over libstdc++ iostream with sync_with_stdio(false) and links raw data (benchmark-results/*.json) and benchmark code (benchmarks/, test.py, which uses g++ -std=c++17 -O2). The runs were on GitHub Actions runners, so no CPU model or gcc version is stated. That makes it first-party with partial methodology, which is C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README: '5x faster than libstdc++ with sync_with_stdio(false);' for reading and writing integers, strings and other primitives (64-bit Linux, gcc, libstdc++). Per-test ratios against iostream_detached in benchmark-results/linux-x86_64.json run from ~1x (line input) to ~80x (bitset input), with a geomean of ~4.7x over 74 test/mode pairs (derived from page data).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: g++ -std=c++17 -O2 (per test.py); gcc version not stated (GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest image)
corrections.hardware: GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest x86_64 runner (per .github/workflows/benchmark.yml); CPU model not stated
corrections.caveats: First-party benchmark run on GitHub Actions runners. The raw data and benchmark code are public, but no CPU model or compiler version is given. The headline 5x is for Linux libstdc++. Raw data also covers macOS (libc++, where the geomean is ~22x) and Windows MSVC (~15x geomean), because iostream is slower there. The speedup varies widely by test, down to ~1x for line reading. The library does not guard against invalid input and targets competitive programming.

notes: The headline claim matches the README, and I checked the ratio against the raw JSON. The record's last_commit (2025-01-16) was the repo's pushed_at; the actual last commit is 2024-11-23, which is still stale.
